source.title: Analysis of Exercise-to-Rest Ratios During Division IA Televised Football Competition

paper.citation: Iosia, M. F., & Bishop, P. A. (2008). Analysis of exercise-to-rest ratios during Division IA televised football competition. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 22(2), 332–340. https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e31816607b0
paper.abstract: What are the durations of offensive plays, rest between plays, and rest between series in televised NCAA Division I-A football, and do they differ by offensive style? Participants: No direct human testing; 423 offensive plays from six televised games were timed. Sport and level: 2004 NCAA Division I-A collegiate American football. Training or return-to-play context: Competition-demand description for conditioning design. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: One game from each of six purposively selected teams; two run-oriented, two pass-oriented, and two balanced offenses; special-teams and defensive plays were excluded. Design: Observational video time-motion analysis. Exposure or intervention: Offensive plays and between-play/series intervals from televised games. Comparator: Run versus pass plays and run-, pass-, and balanced-offense classifications. Measurements and outcomes: Play duration, rest between plays, and rest between offensive series. Analysis: Stopwatch timing from snap to whistle/end of action; inter-rater timing correlations of 0.99 and 0.91; one-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni post-hoc comparisons.
paper.tldr: This observational study informs conditioning design by quantifying play and recovery durations in collegiate American football, while clarifying where competition timing does and does not represent an individual player's physiological load. Across 423 plays, mean play duration was 5.23 ± 1.61 seconds; run plays were shorter than pass plays (4.86 ± 1.41 versus 5.60 ± 1.71 seconds, p = 0.001). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Observational video time-motion analysis. Exposure or intervention: Offensive plays and between-play/series intervals from televised games. Comparator: Run versus pass plays and run-, pass-, and balanced-offense classifications. Measurements and outcomes: Play duration, rest between plays, and rest between offensive series. Analysis: Stopwatch timing from snap to whistle/end of action; inter-rater timing correlations of 0.99 and 0.91; one-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni post-hoc comparisons.
paper.findings: Across 423 plays, mean play duration was 5.23 ± 1.61 seconds; run plays were shorter than pass plays (4.86 ± 1.41 versus 5.60 ± 1.71 seconds, p = 0.001). Mean rest between plays was 46.9 ± 34.3 seconds; after removing extended stoppages, it was 36.09 ± 6.71 seconds. Without extended stoppages, pass-oriented teams had longer between-play rest than run- and balanced-offense teams (38.08 ± 5.85 versus 35.06 ± 6.03 and 35.21 ± 7.71 seconds). Mean rest between offensive series was 11:30 ± 4:19 minutes, with no significant difference by offensive style. The summarized exercise-to-rest ratios ranged from 1:3 in the shortest hurry-up situation to approximately 1:10 with extended rest; the average was approximately 1:7.
paper.limitations: The convenience sample included only one televised game per team from the 2004 season, with offensive style defined by arbitrary season-percentage cutoffs. Timing described the play as a whole and did not identify individual position, movement type, work intensity, substitutions, or defensive and special-teams demands. The authors' conditioning model extrapolated metabolic implications from timing and prior phosphocreatine literature; physiology was not measured in the sampled games. Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): current rules, tempo, broadcast structures, substitutions, and tactical styles may differ from 2004, so these ratios should be refreshed with current team-specific tracking before prescriptive use.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the study as a historical starting range for representative interval design, not as a universal conditioning prescription. Contemporary collegiate American football programming should stratify by position and unit, sample current practice and competition, and preserve skill quality when deciding whether a drill targets repeated high-intensity execution, conditioning overload, or technical development.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, use the study as a historical starting range for representative interval design, not as a universal conditioning prescription. Contemporary collegiate American football programming should stratify by position and unit, sample current practice and competition, and preserve skill quality when deciding whether a drill targets repeated high-intensity execution, conditioning overload, or technical development. Preserve the study population and avoid converting one finding into a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
